body:
Everyone says drift studies ignore the noise floor. The careful ones didn't.

I wrote a paper on this, and the real problem is different: the floor isn't a number you measure. It's a decision about what counts as "the same".

Published monitors declare three different things. Is the name still pointing at the same model? Is the output distribution the same? Is performance on a task the same? Each has its own floor, and different changes clear it.

In one study of 36 model-and-stack combinations (Yang, 2026, not my numbers), the same open model reproduced its own answers 97.5 percent of the time at one cloud provider and 64.5 percent at another.

When I went through the published evidence, the confirmed changes were mostly announced re-pointings of a name, or provider infrastructure events. A capability change under a pinned identifier, with no announced event and a calibrated floor, was not established by any study I found.

That is not "models never change." It is the claim the evidence supports least.

If you monitor an LLM API, declare your null before you collect data:
→ Did the identifier move?
→ Did the output distribution move?
→ Did capability on my task move?
→ Measure the floor on your own task, not someone else's.

The full paper is attached below.
question: When your LLM pipeline's scores shifted, how did you decide whether the model or your measurement moved?
